title: How SuperBalls Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history and science of the Super Ball. They start with a tangent on the Super Bowl's name, which Lamar Hunt reportedly suggested after his kids played with the toy, then move to the Cold War and Sputnik's effect on American science. The main story covers Norman Stingley, a scientist at Bettis Rubber in Whittier, California, who developed the synthetic rubber ball in the late 1960s; the company declined it, and it was then made by Wham-O, which sold it widely. The episode covers knockoffs, the ball's bounce (coefficient of restitution, energy loss as heat), its friction and spin behavior, and its chemistry (Zectron, Polybutadiene). Also includes a listener email correcting the claim that dark and white meat differ by blood vessel count (it is myoglobin content, slow- versus fast-twitch fibers). Much of the opening is off-topic banter about illness, camping, and past episodes.

segments.title: Opening banter and Super Bowl name origin
segments.summary: Hosts chat about being sick and camping, then introduce the Super Bowl name tie-in: Lamar Hunt reportedly suggested the name after his kids played with the Super Ball toy, and the early games were called other names first.

segments.title: Sputnik and Cold War science push
segments.summary: The hosts describe how Sputnik shocked postwar America and pushed scientists to work harder, setting up the story of Norman Stingley.

segments.title: Norman Stingley invents the bouncy rubber ball
segments.summary: Norman Stingley, a scientist at Bettis Rubber in Whittier, California, made a bouncy synthetic rubber ball on his own time. The hosts discuss employee rights to inventions and first refusal. The ball bounced well but broke when thrown hard.

segments.title: Bettis declines; Wham-O takes the ball
segments.summary: Bettis turned the ball down. Stingley took it to Wham-O, which had sold the hula hoop and Frisbee, and the company asked him to improve it.

segments.title: Break and cliffhanger
segments.summary: Short break before the story continues; hosts tease the next part.

segments.title: Knockoffs and chemistry patents
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the patent on the Zectron process, how slightly altered formulas can avoid it, and an analogy to music sampling. They then discuss how cheap knockoff Super Balls spread.

segments.title: Super Ball size, bounce, and energy
segments.summary: The regular Super Ball measured about 1.875 inches across, slightly bigger than a racquetball, and was made with Zectron. It dropped from twelve inches and rebounded to ten inches, then nine point seven, eight point seven five. The hosts explain the coefficient of restitution and the roughly ten percent energy loss to heat on each impact.

segments.title: Super Ball friction, spin, and chemistry
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Super Ball's high friction, which changes spin on contact so the ball can come back at the thrower, and mention polybutadiene as the base chemistry.

segments.title: Sign-off on Super Balls
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the Super Ball story, credit Norman Stingley, and point listeners to the search bar on the website.

segments.title: Listener mail: dark meat versus white meat
segments.summary: A listener writes that the color difference between dark and white meat comes from myoglobin content and fiber type (slow-twitch versus fast-twitch), not blood vessel count. The hosts accept the correction.

segments.title: Sign-off and social media
segments.summary: Hosts give social media handles and the website address, and sign off.
